title: The Box Worth More Than Its Contents

beats.text: In nineteen twenty-nine, Wall Street sold boxes of stocks for more than what's inside.
December nineteen twenty-eight. Goldman Sachs opens a trust, a company that only owns other shares.
You pay a hundred and four dollars for about a hundred dollars of stocks.
Within weeks, your shares more than double.
So how is a box worth more than its contents?
Nobody asks. That summer, the trust launches a trust, which launches another.
A trust owning a trust owning a trust, on borrowed money.
You see, it's a fruit basket. The bow costs extra.
Now baskets hold baskets, some bought with a loan.
The fruit slips a little, the loan doesn't, so the top baskets crash.
And the bow you paid extra for? Gone first.
By nineteen thirty-two, the market had lost nearly ninety percent.
Your hundred-and-four-dollar share? A dollar seventy-five. The baskets fell further than the fruit.

facts.claim: Goldman Sachs launched the Goldman Sachs Trading Corporation, an investment trust (closed-end fund), in December 1928 (Dec 4, 1928)
Shares were offered to the public at $104 each (one million shares)
Behind each share sat about $100 of assets: Goldman bought the 1,000,000-share issue for $100 million; net asset value around $100 million (GS: $50M capital + $50M surplus)

Within weeks (early 1929) the shares more than doubled: GS history 'within three days shares had more than doubled over their initial value'; Novel Investor: $222.50 two months after launch, double its asset value
1929 investment trusts traded at premiums above the value of the stocks they held (median seasoned-fund premium ~47-50% in Q3 1929; GSTC at double asset value)
In July and August 1929 the trust launched Shenandoah Corporation, which in turn launched Blue Ridge Corporation (Shenandoah's capital used to buy Blue Ridge)
The structure was interlocking and highly leveraged (debt and preferred stock; 'a premium to a premium to a premium')
Premiums vanished: by end of 1929 GSTC and most seasoned funds traded below net asset value (median discount 8% in Dec 1929)
By 1932 stocks had lost nearly 90 percent of their value (Dow 381.2 in Sept 1929)
GSTC shares (split-adjusted) fell to $1.75 by mid-1932

caption:
December 1928: the Goldman Sachs Trading Corporation sold shares at $104 for about $100 of stocks, and within weeks they more than doubled.
Then the trust launched a trust that launched another, stacked on borrowed money. By 1932 the share was $1.75.
